          Kane, Yamal, Mbappé or Messi: Who Should Win the 2026 Men's Ballon d'Or?
        
      
                          
                      Oct 23, 2026
          
                      Ryan Benson / Author, Emily Millen / Design
                  
      
              
                      
                  
          

    
              
      
              
                    
Thirty players are on the shortlist for the 2026 Men's Ballon d'Or, but who's actually in contention for the award?
Who will win the 2026 Men's Ballon d'Or? Well, we don't have to wait much longer to find out.
The ceremony will take place on Monday, crowning one player as the best in the world based on their performances between 3 August 2025 and 19 July 2026.
The shortlist for the men's award stands at 30 strong and includes three former winners: Ousmane Dembélé (2025), Rodri (2024) and Lionel Messi (2009, 2010, 2011, 2012, 2015, 2019, 2021, 2023).

But some have far more realistic chances of winning this year's prize than others. Ahead of Monday's ceremony, it would seem there are four clear frontrunners; here, we assess their respective chances.

It may not count for much given Vinícius Júnior was hotly tipped before losing out to Rodri in the 2024 Ballon d’Or, but ahead of Monday’s ceremony, Harry Kane is the favourite to take home the prize this year.
That might even be something of a surprise to many. Not because there’s any doubt about just how good Kane is, rather that he would buck a fairly established trend.

In World Cup years since the start of the 1990s, there have only been two instances of a player not winning the Champions League/European Cup or being a world champion but taking home the Ballon d’Or: Hristo Stoichkov in 1994 and Messi in 2010.

Not that he had a bad year on either front. His Bayern Munich side reached the semi-finals of the Champions League, while he captained England to the last four of the World Cup. And, unsurprisingly, he played a major role in both runs.
Kane scored 14 times for Bayern in the Champions League, bettered only by Kylian Mbappé (15), and he netted six in the World Cup; just four players scored more.
Kane’s 14 UCL goals came amid a generally exceptional season at club level, helping Bayern stroll to the Bundesliga title with a 16-point cushion and success in the DFB-Pokal.

He scored 61 times in 51 appearances across all competitions, 19 more than anyone else playing in the top five European leagues; in fact, the only player to net more in a single campaign for a club from one of Europe’s top leagues was Messi (73) in 2011-12.
Thirty-six of Kane’s 61-goal haul came in the Bundesliga, securing him the European Golden Shoe for a second time, with only Messi (6) and Cristiano Ronaldo (4) having won it more often.
Although Kane won’t have won the prize while playing for a Premier League club if he is ultimately crowned on Monday, such a success would be momentous for English football.
No English player has won the Ballon d’Or since Michael Owen in 2001. Before him, the country’s only recipients were Kevin Keegan (1978 and 1979) and Bobby Charlton (1966).

It’s fair to say Kane’s decision to leave Tottenham – and specifically for Bayern – has long been vindicated from a trophies perspective. Winning the Ballon d’Or would provide him with the ultimate personal recognition that would probably have never arrived if he’d stayed at Spurs.

The most realistic challenger to Kane’s Ballon d’Or bid? It seems that way; he did win the World Cup after all, and as noted before, football’s biggest individual prize is ordinarily won by a world champion on applicable years.
It also shouldn’t be forgotten that Lamine Yamal enjoyed an excellent 2025-26 season at club level with Barcelona. But, like Kane, he didn’t win the Champions League.

For some voters, the very fact Yamal was in the World Cup-winning Spain side will have been enough to earn points. For others, though, the question being asked will be how critical was his contribution to Spain’s glory?

Obviously it’s pretty difficult to work this out definitively; an attacker may not record many goals or assists but their input could have still been vital for many goals. But people will, most of the time, be led by the topline numbers.
